If the problematic result is `Indeterminate`, you can replace it after the computation:

`expr /. Indeterminate -> 0`

This turns any `Indeterminate` value into `0`, including cases where a sum or list element evaluates to `Indeterminate`. If you are using a function and then summing its results, you can apply the same replacement to those results before summing.

The variable on the left side of a function definition is a pattern, not the same as a global variable. Matching happens before `x` is evaluated, so a definition like `x = 5 y; function1[y_] := x` will not automatically use the later value of `x` when you call `function1[5]`.

If you want the current value of `x` baked into the rule, define the function after substituting the value, for example:

`(function1[y_] := {#, y}) &@x`

This forces `x` to be turned into `5 y` before the definition is stored.

ReplaceAll works outside-in. That means it can match the outermost expression first and then stop there, so inner parts may never be reached if the outer match succeeds. That is why it can seem like only the top level changes.

If you need both outer and inner parts transformed, use Replace with a level specification like {0, Infinity}. For example:

Replace[a[b[c, d]], head_[arg__] :> newHead[arg], {0, Infinity}]

This transforms both levels and returns:

newHead[newHead[c, d]]

So the behavior comes from ReplaceAll’s outside-in matching strategy.

Use `InputField` with a `Dynamic` string variable. If you want the Return key to insert a newline, wrap the field in `EventHandler` and handle `"ReturnKeyDown"`.

For example:

```wl
DynamicModule[{input = ""},
 Column[{
   TextCell["Enter your text here:"],
   EventHandler[
    InputField[Dynamic[input], String, ContinuousAction -> True, FieldSize -> {40, 7}],
    "ReturnKeyDown" :> FrontEndExecute[{NotebookWrite[InputNotebook[], "\n", After]}]
   ],
   Dynamic@InputForm[input]
 }]
]
```

This gives free-form text entry and adds a newline on Return.

pts = Cases[ContourPlot[f[x, z] == 0, {x, xmin, xmax}, {z, zmin, zmax}],

If you want the points returned from a ContourPlot, use the contour curves as implicit equations and solve their intersections with Reduce or Solve, then extract the coordinates.

For example, for the two contours:
y^2 - 2 x^2 (x + 3) == 0
y^2 - 2 x^2 (x + 3) == 2 ((y + 1)^2 (y + 9) - x^2)

you can do:
Reduce[{eq1, eq2}, {x, y}, Reals]

or numerically:
NSolve[{eq1, eq2}, {x, y}, Reals]

That returns the {x, y} points directly. The evidence also shows N@Reduce gives approximate real x-values for the intersections, with y-values obtained from the same solution. If you mean the actual sampled points produced by ContourPlot itself, that is not covered here.

`MatchQ` evaluates its arguments before matching, so if you write `MatchQ[Function[], ...]` the `Function[]` part will be evaluated first unless you prevent it.

To control that, hold the expression you want to test, or wrap it so it is not evaluated before `MatchQ` sees it. The earlier case shows this issue: without holding, you end up comparing the evaluated result instead of the original pattern.

Also, if you mean “a no-argument expression whose head is a pattern variable,” the supported form is `x_[]`, not `x[]`.

Use `MatchQ` on a held form of the expression you want to test, then decide whether to evaluate the argument separately. The supported pattern from the example is to match the argument sequence as a list and test it with `MatchQ[{x}, ...]`, e.g.

`mol[x__] := With[{}, Message[mol::arg] /; ! MatchQ[{x}, {Subscript[_String, _Integer] ..}]]`

This lets you control when the argument is examined, instead of relying on `Except[...]` to match multiple arguments. The evidence does not show a specific `Function[]` pattern for `MatchQ`, but it supports using a held wrapper plus `MatchQ` on `{x}` to avoid unwanted evaluation.

`doThat[expr_, vars_List] := Expand[Simplify[expr /. Flatten[Solve[# == ToString@#, First@Variables@#] & /@ vars]], Alternatives @@ ToString /@ vars] /. Thread[ToString /@ vars -> vars]`

So for:
`doThat[c a (x1 + x2) + d a (x1 + x2) + a (y1 + y2), {x1 + x2, y1 + y2}]`

it returns:
